title: YouTube as a source of information on COVID-19: a pandemic of misinformation?
screen_reason: Cross-sectional analysis of the 69 most-viewed English-language YouTube videos on COVID-19 (search of 21 March 2020, top 75 videos for each of 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19'). Two independent reviewers classified each video factual vs non-factual against WHO/CDC guidance current at the video's publication date (Cohen's kappa 0.86). Reports both the share of videos containing non-factual information (19/69 = 27.5 %) and the share of the corpus's observed viewership those videos received (62,042,609 of 257,804,146 views = 24.1 %). Item-level falsity against an external ground truth with a denominator = CONTENT; the viewership-weighted share has a consumption denominator (observed view counts) = EXPOSURE. The CSS, mDISCERN and mJAMA instruments are reported only as means and yield no shares.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube videos; authors based in Ottawa, Canada)
estimates.measure_type: % of the most-viewed English-language YouTube COVID-19 videos that contained non-factual (misleading) information
estimates.value_raw: 19 (27.5%) of 69 included videos contained non-factual information; 50 (72.5%) contained only factual information
estimates.denominator: 69 videos included from the 150 most-viewed videos screened (top 75 by views for each of the keywords 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19'); 81 excluded as duplicates (42), non-English (31), over 1 hour (4), live streams (1), no audio (2) or unrelated (1)
estimates.definition: video contained one or more non-factual statements, judged against guidelines from major public health agencies (e.g. WHO, CDC) as they stood at the video's publication date
estimates.misinfo_def: Videos were considered non-factual if they contained one or more non-factual statements, as evaluated based on guidelines from major public health agencies (eg, WHO and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) at the video's publication date.
estimates.source_quote: Of the 69 included videos, 19 (27.5%) contained non-­ factual information, while 50 (72.5%) contained only factual information. Cohen’s kappa for the categorisa- tion of factual and misleading videos was 0.86±0.07.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Factual versus non-factual videos', p. 3; Table 1; abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two reviewers (HO-YL, AB) independently reviewed and coded all 150 videos in duplicate, categorising them factual vs non-factual against major public health agency guidance (WHO, CDC) current at each video's publication date; discrepancies resolved by a third reviewer (DH) and the senior author (JC) by consensus. Cohen's kappa 0.86 (SD 0.07) for the factual/misleading categorisation and 0.90 (SD 0.04) for source categorisation.
estimates.moderator_quote: A YouTube search was performed on 21 March 2020 using the keywords 'coronavirus' and 'COVID-19'. The search was done using a cleared-cache web browser ... Search results were sorted by 'views' to obtain the most widely viewed YouTube videos in descending order at the time of search. The hyperlinks of most widely viewed 75 videos for each keyword were collected on a spreadsheet for data collection.
estimates.notes: Rank-truncated most-viewed sample (top 75 per keyword), hence denom_scope=topical with denom_selection=curated - this is a high-attention slice of COVID-19 YouTube, not a random sample of the platform's COVID content, and English-only. The falsity threshold is lenient (one or more non-factual statements makes the whole video non-factual), which inflates the video-level share relative to a statement-level measure; the paper is explicit about it. Only 46 % of screened videos survived the exclusions.

estimates.country: Not stated (English-language YouTube videos; authors based in Ottawa, Canada)
estimates.date: search performed 21 March 2020 (view counts as of that date)
estimates.measure_type: % of total views of the most-viewed English-language YouTube COVID-19 videos that went to videos containing non-factual information
estimates.value_raw: 62 042 609 (24.1) non-factual views vs 195 761 537 (75.9) factual views, of 257 804 146 total views [Table 1]
estimates.denominator: 257,804,146 views accumulated by the 69 included most-viewed English-language COVID-19 videos as of 21 March 2020
estimates.definition: views of videos containing one or more non-factual statements (judged against WHO/CDC guidance), as a share of all views of the 69-video corpus
estimates.misinfo_def: Videos were considered non-factual if they contained one or more non-factual statements, as evaluated based on guidelines from major public health agencies (eg, WHO and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention) at the video's publication date.
estimates.source_quote: Non-­ factual videos accounted for 24.1% of the total viewership for a total of 62 042 609 views. Factual videos accounted for 75.9% of total viewership.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Factual versus non-factual videos', p. 3; Table 1 (# of views row)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same duplicate coding by two reviewers against WHO/CDC guidance, kappa 0.86; view counts taken from YouTube's own displayed counts at the time of search (observed views, not modelled reach).
estimates.moderator_quote: The total viewership of the 69 included videos was 257 804 146 views.
estimates.notes: Same 69-video corpus as the 27.5 % row, weighted by observed views instead of counted by item - the two rows are not independent estimates and must not be pooled together. The denominator is views within this curated top-viewed set, so it is a share of attention to these videos, NOT a share of anyone's total media or COVID-news diet. Views are cumulative lifetime counts at the search date, and one video can be watched repeatedly by the same person, so this is a view-share, not a person-reach.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) SOURCE-CATEGORY SUBGROUPS NOT ROWED: within-category shares of non-factual videos are reported (internet news 63 % (5/8), entertainment news 60 % (6/10), consumer 33 % (3/9), network news 20 % (5/30), professional/government 0 % (0/7), newspaper 0 % (0/3), education 0 % (0/2)). These are producer-type subgroups of the same 69-video corpus, not a country/platform/measure split and not the paper's headline, so per the collapse rule I kept the whole-corpus figure. Note a printing inconsistency in Table 1 for internet news: '5 (63)' non-factual and '3 (60)' factual, where the factual cell should read 37 %. (2) COMPOSITION OF THE MISINFORMATION SET, not prevalence: of the 19 non-factual videos, 6 entertainment news (32 %), 5 network news (26 %), 5 internet news (26 %), 3 consumer (13 %). This is a within-misinformation breakdown (R3 territory), not a share of a full denominator. (3) VIEWERSHIP BY SOURCE (Table 2: network news 29 %, consumer 22 %, entertainment news 21 %, internet news 12 %, professional 7 %, newspaper 5 %, education 2 %, government 2 %) describes the composition of viewing across producers, with no misinformation numerator. (4) QUALITY INSTRUMENTS: CSS, mDISCERN and mJAMA are reported only as means with SDs (e.g. non-factual videos mDISCERN 1.16±1.17 vs factual 3.50±1.22); no share of videos above any threshold is given, so no QUALITY row could be made. (5) The 23 %-26.3 % figures for H1N1/Ebola/Zika in the introduction and key-questions box are values cited from other papers (refs 8-10) and are excluded by R8. (6) No country is reported for the videos or their audiences; English-only inclusion is a stated limitation.

rob.design: Cross-sectional single-time-point YouTube content analysis. Frame: the 75 most-viewed videos for each of two keywords ('coronavirus', 'COVID-19') on 21 March 2020, searched in a cleared-cache Chrome incognito session and sorted by views; of 150 screened, 69 (46 %) included after a priori exclusions (duplicates 42, non-English 31, >1 hour 4, live 1, no audio 2, unrelated 1). Coding: two reviewers independently coded all videos in duplicate for source category, factual/non-factual status, and CSS/mDISCERN/mJAMA; disagreements resolved by a third reviewer and the senior author. Reliability reported: Cohen's kappa 0.86 (SD 0.07) for factual vs misleading, 0.90 (SD 0.04) for source category. Stated limitations: single time point on a dynamic platform, English-only language bias, the CSS instrument is novel and unvalidated, and only YouTube-hosted copies were captured. No funding; no competing interests declared.
